setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
claim: The current public NCG VTB page describes a host-and-centre model, deadline-based case submission, scheduled videoconference discussion, and a downloadable presentation template, but does not describe a public post-meeting decision handoff or follow-through process.
source_title: The Virtual Tumor Board (VTB)
supporting_extract: Member centres submit cases before recurring Wednesday or Saturday sessions; host centres run sessions and experts contribute. The page provides participation, submission, hosting, equipment, schedule, and template information, but no public post-meeting workflow.
method_sample: Direct review of the current official programme page.
limitations: The page may lag actual operating practice; absence of public documentation is not proof that no internal decision or follow-up process exists.
frequency_evidence: Recurring Wednesday and Saturday sessions are listed; case throughput is not reported.
burden_evidence: Submission deadlines imply coordination but no person-time, rejection, postponement, or follow-through burden is measured.
current_workaround: Case presentation is submitted to programme coordination and discussed by videoconference under a host-centre model.
existing_solution: NCG VTB provides recurring sessions, expert participation, coordination, and a presentation template.
contradiction: The existing national programme already solves scheduling and access to a board; a new generic board would duplicate it.
implication: Investigate only a specific post-meeting operational handoff and never infer non-existence from undocumented public pages.
unknowns: Actual post-meeting decision record, recipient, responsible actor, assignment, acknowledgement, due state, and completion tracking.
provenance_notes: Public contact details and clinical case examples were deliberately excluded; same source group as EV-0020, not independent confirmation.

setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
claim: The public NCG VTB presentation template structures presenter and centre information, diagnosis, brief presentation and examination, treatment history, investigations, imaging, treatment fitness where relevant, and questions for the board; it contains no visible decision, owner, due-date, communication, or completion fields.
source_title: NCG Virtual Tumor Board presentation template
supporting_extract: The six-slide blank template ends with questions for the tumour board after brief history, investigations, imaging, and fitness sections.
method_sample: Direct extraction of the public blank PowerPoint template; six slides reviewed.
limitations: A presentation template may be only one part of the workflow and may intentionally omit internal minutes, EMR entries, or post-meeting systems.
frequency_evidence: Template is linked for recurring VTB submission; actual usage and completion rates are not reported.
burden_evidence: No preparation time, missing-field rate, or rejection rate is reported.
current_workaround: Presenters prepare a slide deck using the published template.
existing_solution: A standardised public case-presentation artifact already exists.
contradiction: Pre-board structure is not absent; novelty must come from an evidenced handoff rather than recreating the case form.
implication: Treat the template as a possible input boundary, not a product to replace; seek the separate human decision and operational disposition artifacts.
unknowns: Whether a decision/minutes template exists privately, who authors it, who receives it, and how actions are tracked.
provenance_notes: No filled case, patient data, presenter name, centre name, or contact detail was collected.

claim: iECHO participant guidance describes invitation-based case upload into a selected session, programme-team review, approval or rejection, and re-upload after a stated rejection reason.
source_title: Submitting a case presentation
supporting_extract: The participant follows a hub invitation, selects the participant group and session Content area, uploads a file, and waits for programme-team approval or rejection; rejected submissions can be corrected and re-uploaded after email or SMS notice.
method_sample: Direct browser review of the public iECHO participant help article.
limitations: Generic iECHO guidance, not an NCG-specific usage audit; it documents pre-session content handling and says nothing about post-board decisions.
frequency_evidence: No NCG case count, rejection rate, or turnaround is reported.
burden_evidence: Revision loop exists but no frequency or time burden is reported.
current_workaround: Invitation, session-specific file upload, review, rejection reason, notification, and re-upload.
existing_solution: iECHO already supplies a review-state workflow for pre-session case content.
contradiction: A basic upload, review, and notification product would duplicate the current platform.
implication: Do not rebuild pre-board file review; test whether the post-board decision-to-action handoff is outside this documented workflow.
unknowns: NCG configuration, decision capture, post-session distribution, action assignment, outcome tracking, and retention rules.
provenance_notes: Page content was read through a browser because static extraction returned only the hosting shell; no account or private programme was accessed.

claim: iECHO hub guidance assigns the organisation team responsibility for choosing case presenters, reviewing uploaded content, checking for PII or PHI, approving or rejecting it, and sharing approved content with participants.
source_title: How to add a Case presenter
supporting_extract: The organisation team assigns active participants as presenters; the platform notifies them, keeps uploads under review, supports download and approve or reject, sends a rejection reason, and shares approved files. The guidance recommends PHI and PII review.
method_sample: Direct browser review of the public iECHO hub help article.
limitations: Generic platform documentation, not evidence that NCG uses every feature or that the organisation team owns post-board actions.
frequency_evidence: Multiple presenters are supported; usage rates are not reported.
burden_evidence: No review time, rejection rate, privacy incident rate, or workload measure is reported.
current_workaround: Organisation or programme staff administer presenter assignment and content approval in iECHO.
existing_solution: A pre-board operational owner, review states, notifications, privacy check, and controlled sharing already exist in the platform.
contradiction: The pre-board actor and review workflow are clearer than the post-board problem; Candidate B should not bundle both without evidence.
implication: Treat the organisation/programme team as a known pre-board actor only; keep the post-board owner unresolved.
unknowns: Which NCG role performs this work, whether the same role records decisions, and what happens after the session ends.
provenance_notes: Same iECHO help source group as EV-0038; public guidance only, with no user account or patient content.

subproblem: NCG VTB operating roles and platform migration
setting: National Cancer Grid Virtual Tumor Board
workflow_moment: case intake review scheduling and presentation
claim: An NCG 2022 programme account says participants submitted weekly case presentations to an ECHO-appointed coordinator working with NCG experts, disease-management groups reviewed presentations before spokes presented, and VTBs moved to iECHO to streamline scheduling and produce more programme metrics.
source_title: NCG Newsletter Issue 4 — Virtual Tumor Board activity
supporting_extract: The programme account identifies a coordinator, expert review, disease-site groups, invited presentation, videoconference operation, and an October 2022 migration to iECHO for streamlined scheduling and more programme metrics.
method_sample: Direct review of the official NCG newsletter feature describing programme operations through 2022.
limitations: Historical programme description; named contacts and current platform configuration may have changed; post-meeting decision ownership is not described.
frequency_evidence: The source describes weekly submissions and recurring programmes, with historical attendance summaries but no current throughput retained here.
burden_evidence: No coordinator time, review delay, rejection rate, or action-follow-up measure is reported.
current_workaround: Coordinator intake, NCG expert and disease-group review, invited presentation, and iECHO-supported sessions.
existing_solution: NCG and ECHO India already provide programme coordination, review, scheduling, and platform operations.
contradiction: National coordination and pre-board review are established; the unmet step must be narrower and current.
implication: Coordinator is evidenced for pre-board intake, not post-board accountability; verify current roles before naming a product user.
unknowns: Current coordinator arrangement, post-meeting decision artifact, treating-team acknowledgement, action assignment, and outcome visibility.
provenance_notes: Public personal contact details in the newsletter were not copied; this source does not independently prove current practice.

subproblem: formal MDT coordinator role transfer evidence
workflow_moment: meeting preparation minutes distribution and pathway follow-through
claim: A formal NHS regional guideline assigns an MDT coordinator responsibility for meeting coordination, advance lists and evidence, attendance and minutes, distributing notes, producing agreed action plans and reviews, recording data, monitoring milestones, and escalating delays.
source_title: Policy and Guidelines for Investigation, Diagnosis and Management of Malignancy of Unknown Origin and Cancer of Unknown Primary
publisher: NHS England West Midlands Clinical Networks
supporting_extract: The coordinator duties include preparing patient lists and evidence, taking and distributing minutes, ensuring diagnoses and plans enter notes, producing action plans with agreed reviews, monitoring milestones, reporting, and escalating delays.
method_sample: Official regional policy for a specific NHS cancer pathway; responsibilities section reviewed directly.
limitations: England, CUP-specific, published in 2018 and expired for local review in 2018; role design cannot be assumed for Indian boards.
frequency_evidence: Defines recurring role responsibilities but reports no workload frequency.
burden_evidence: No time, caseload, or effect size is reported.
current_workaround: A dedicated coordinator maintains meeting artifacts, communication, action plans, pathway data, and escalation.
existing_solution: Formal coordinator-led MDT operations demonstrate that decision-to-action ownership is an established workflow pattern elsewhere.
contradiction: This evidence may describe a staffing and governance function rather than a software gap, and cannot name the Indian owner.
implication: Use coordinator as a role hypothesis and interview target, not as an India-specific fact or automatic product user.
unknowns: Whether Indian hospitals assign equivalent duties, whether one person owns them, and which tasks are unmet versus manually adequate.
provenance_notes: No patient, staff contact, or local identifier retained; geographic and currency limits are explicit.

workflow_moment: case selection scheduling review attendance and decision documentation
claim: A draft NABH oncology HIS/EMR annexure specifies tumour-board patient selection, unique board ID, scheduling, clinician notifications, a central case list, integrated record review, attendance, and documentation of multidisciplinary inputs, recommendations, and follow-ups; it does not specify an operational acknowledgement, action owner, due date, or intermediate completion state.
source_title: NABH Digital Health Standards for HIS EMR Systems — Annexure for Cancer Care and Management
publisher: National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers
supporting_extract: MDC 1(a) requires patient selection, tumour-board ID assignment, review scheduling, and clinician notifications; 1(b) describes a central scheduled-patient view; 1(c) records attendance; 1(d) documents multidisciplinary diagnosis, treatment-recommendation, and follow-up inputs in a standardised summary.
method_sample: Draft Indian digital-health certification annexure for oncology HIS/EMR systems; its multidisciplinary-care section defines four tumour-board objective elements.
limitations: Draft status and publication date are not stated in the document; requirements are not evidence of implementation or burden. The referenced sample summary is marked as annexure XXX. Clinical recommendation content exceeds this project's product boundary.
frequency_evidence: No frequency or adoption measurement is reported.
burden_evidence: No person-time, delay, missing-data, acknowledgement, or completion baseline is reported.
current_workaround: Not measured; the annexure describes intended HIS/EMR capability rather than current local practice.
existing_solution: NABH's draft standard already defines a substantial electronic tumour-board workflow and overlaps NCG/KCDO requirements.
contradiction: Weakens novelty for a broad tumour-board module and shows that public standards already expect scheduling, integrated review, attendance, and decision/follow-up documentation; it does not establish the proposed intermediate handoff gap.
implication: Validate only the narrow post-decision acknowledgement and operational-status handoff against actual implementations; do not recreate the standard's broad board workflow.
unknowns: Whether the draft was finalised or implemented; whether certified systems capture acknowledgement, owner, due date, and completion; how follow-up is defined locally.
provenance_notes: Direct reading of the public NABH-hosted draft PDF on 2026-09-03; clinical recommendation text is retained only to describe the standard and is not promoted as product scope.

subproblem: single-centre post-board spreadsheet and coordinator workflow
workflow_moment: weekly case listing decision entry and post-board treatment follow-up collection
claim: A one-year Eastern India tumour-board audit used preformed Excel case lists, entered the board's management decision after each meeting, and used a patient care coordinator to collect later treatment and follow-up information, trace unreachable patients, and complete a master chart.
source_title: Incorporation of a Multidisciplinary Tumor Board in Cancer Patient Care: Experiences of a Comprehensive Cancer Care Hospital in Eastern India
publisher: Asian Pacific Journal of Cancer Care
supporting_extract: The weekly board prepared case lists beforehand on preformed Excel sheets; after the meeting the recommended management plan was entered. Treatment details and follow-up data were then collected from hospital records with help from a patient care coordinator, who attempted to trace patients and complete the master chart.
method_sample: Prospective before-and-after data collection for a 12-month single-centre audit, August 2020 to July 2021; 800 case discussions, including 573 new cases and 227 repeat discussions.
limitations: Single private hospital; audit workflow may not represent routine operations elsewhere. The study measures treatment and follow-up data completeness, not treating-unit acknowledgement, coordinator person-time, or product effectiveness. More than 20% of some data remained missing.
frequency_evidence: The board met weekly and recorded 800 discussions in 12 months; 28.37% were repeat discussions.
burden_evidence: The audit reports 20.75% unknown treatment status, 31.5% lost to follow-up at analysis, and 20.37% missing staging data, but no staff person-time or decision-acknowledgement rate.
current_workaround: Preformed Excel case list and master chart, repeated checking, hospital-record review, and patient care coordinator tracing.
existing_solution: A named patient care coordinator plus spreadsheet-based board register and follow-up collection operated at this hospital.
contradiction: Provides one direct Indian actor and post-board workflow, showing that staffing and a spreadsheet may already own the task; however substantial missing and unknown data persisted. It does not prove a decision-to-treating-unit acknowledgement gap.
implication: The patient care coordinator is a plausible operator in some hospitals. P5 should test whether the initial job is decision entry, treating-unit acknowledgement, or later data collection, and whether a lightweight improvement removes rather than duplicates the spreadsheet.
unknowns: Who entered the board decision; whether the treating unit acknowledged it; which fields existed in the preformed sheet; coordinator time; reasons for missing data; current workflow after the 2020–2021 audit.
provenance_notes: Direct reading of the journal landing page and full article PDF on 2026-09-03. No patient-level data or author contact details were retained.

subproblem: current Indian post-MDT referral and documentation quality improvement
workflow_moment: post-MDT identification referral documentation access and later review
claim: A 2023–2025 NCG EQuIP-India quality-improvement project identified eligible patients during MDT meetings, assigned the treating oncologist to initiate a goals-of-care discussion and referral, and assigned the palliative-care team to complete and document it. A standard operating procedure and one colour-coded paper form replaced unreliable verbal handoff and raised documentation from 0% to 92% in the 26-patient target cohort.
source_title: Initiating and Documenting Goals of Care Discussion in Patients with Advanced Pancreatic and Colorectal Cancers: A Quality Improvement Project in a Low Resource Setting
supporting_extract: The project identified patients during MDT meetings; treating oncologists initiated the discussion and referred to pain and palliative care, whose team completed and documented it. Verbal communication failed because teams worked in different buildings and were not always reachable. A combined colour-coded form with checkboxes and an SOP produced 24 documented discussions among 26 eligible patients.
method_sample: Single-centre A3/PDSA quality-improvement project at Cancer Institute (WIA), Chennai. Ran September 2023 to May 2024, followed to March 2025; target cohort was 26 people with advanced pancreatic or colorectal cancer selected under clinician-defined criteria.
limitations: This is a sensitive clinical goals-of-care workflow, not a generic tumour-board decision-handoff study. Eligibility and content require clinical judgement and are outside this product boundary. Single institution and small target cohort; no treating-unit acknowledgement measure or coordinator person-time. The successful intervention was process, training, SOP, and paper documentation; a digital EMR version was not implemented.
frequency_evidence: Twenty-six eligible cases were identified during the target project; the authors later report 176 additional referrals beyond the original cancer groups. These counts do not establish generic tumour-board volume.
burden_evidence: Baseline goals-of-care documentation was 0%; 24 of 26 eligible target cases were documented after intervention, reported as 92%. The study names coordination, record-location, and communication barriers but does not quantify staff person-time.
current_workaround: Isolated poorly documented discussions and unreliable verbal/telephone referral were replaced by a shared colour-coded paper chart document, patient-handbook sticker, SOP, eligibility criteria, and repeated resident education.
existing_solution: A clearly divided human workflow—oncologist initiates and refers; palliative-care team discusses and documents—plus a standard paper form and SOP achieved the stated documentation result without a new software product.
contradiction: A concrete recent Indian post-MDT handoff was owned by downstream clinical teams rather than a generic board secretariat and improved primarily through governance, role clarity, training, and one paper artifact. This weakens the assumption that a reusable software layer or universal tumour-board operational owner is the primary need.
implication: Use only the operational pattern as transfer evidence: name the downstream owner, define the trigger, unify the handoff artifact, and measure documentation. Do not build around goals-of-care eligibility, clinical discussion, prognosis, or treatment. Candidate B must show a current non-clinical gap that process and an existing form cannot solve.
unknowns: Whether the paper workflow remains current after the planned EMR transition; whether a board record was separately acknowledged by the treating unit; staff time; applicability outside this sensitive clinical pathway; whether other sites assign secretariat, treating-team, or downstream-service ownership.
provenance_notes: Direct reading of the complete PubMed Central article on 2026-09-03. No patient-level data, author contact details, or supplementary clinical form contents were retained.

workflow_moment: family support during diagnosis treatment and follow-up
claim: Two of three informal caregiver accounts describe absent or inadequate family counselling or psychosocial support, suggesting a possible service-access and coordination gap rather than evidence for automated advice.
source_title: De-identified analysis of the expanded pain-point source
supporting_extract: Two selected caregiver accounts describe family-support or counselling needs that were absent or inadequately addressed; this public record intentionally omits narrative and clinical detail.
method_sample: Three unstructured caregiver accounts embedded in a private team document; no recruitment method, interview instrument, sampling frame, or contemporaneous note method is reported.
limitations: Selected small sample, sensitive raw narratives, unclear authorship and provenance, no clinician confirmation, no denominator, and no frequency, role, service, or outcome measurement. The accounts cannot establish prevalence.
frequency_evidence: The signal appears in two of three selected accounts; this is within-source recurrence, not a population rate or independent confirmation.
burden_evidence: No staff time, caregiver time, access delay, completion rate, or service baseline is reported.
current_workaround: Families appear to navigate support informally; the specific services, referrals, and ownership are not reported consistently.
existing_solution: Human counselling, psychosocial support, navigation, or clinician-approved education may exist, but availability and workflow are not established by this source.
contradiction: The accounts expose a plausible need but do not show that software is the intervention; human service capacity, role clarity, referral, or approved information may be primary.
implication: Add caregiver and family psychosocial-support coordination to the outside-theme scan. Promote only an operational service-access workflow if a named role, recurring trigger, safe output, baseline, and human clinical boundary are established.
unknowns: Responsible role; service availability; consent and permissions; frequency; unmet-demand denominator; safe operational output; whether the problem is information, referral, capacity, language, or counselling quality.
provenance_notes: De-identified paraphrase from a fully reviewed owner-supplied private DOCX. Raw narratives, quotations, ages, dates, institutions, diagnoses, family history, and care details are deliberately excluded. All records from this document share one source group.

subproblem: cross-city referral additional-opinion and multi-provider records
workflow_moment: referral additional opinion and transfer between providers
claim: The selected caregiver accounts include cross-city referral, additional opinions, and care involving multiple providers, weakening the earlier informal assumption that oncology journeys rarely change doctors or institutions.
source_title: De-identified analysis of the expanded pain-point source
supporting_extract: The small account set contains de-identified examples of referrals, additional opinions, cross-city movement, and multiple providers; exact journeys and clinical details are not reproduced.
method_sample: Three unstructured caregiver accounts in a private team document; selected sample with no prevalence design or standard workflow questions.
limitations: Small selected sample, unclear recruitment and chronology, no actor/time measurement, and no evidence that all source artifacts moved or required reconciliation. It cannot estimate how often oncology care changes providers.
frequency_evidence: Examples occur within a three-account source set; no denominator beyond the selected accounts and no population estimate exist.
burden_evidence: No preparation person-time, missing-record rate, clarification count, delay, or correction rate is reported.
current_workaround: Caregivers and patients carried or navigated records and appointments across providers; exact institutional exchange and verification steps are not reported.
existing_solution: Paper and patient-carried records, local digital records, referral processes, EMRs, and ABDM-aligned exchange may address parts of the journey; adequacy is unknown.
contradiction: Contradicts the blanket informal assumption that oncologist switching or additional opinions are generally too rare to matter, but does not prove Candidate A's frequency, burden, or product fit.
implication: Increase the priority of measuring Candidate A's referral and outside-record workflow, while retaining the need for a named preparer, total person-time, verification cost, and existing-system comparison.
unknowns: Frequency by setting; exact preparer; artifact set; source authority; repeat-testing versus record-transfer cause; total staff/caregiver time; current ABDM/EMR capability; safe consultation output.
provenance_notes: De-identified paraphrase from a fully reviewed owner-supplied private DOCX. No exact journey, quotation, person, date, institution, diagnosis, or location combination is retained. Shares one source group with EV-0045, EV-0047, and EV-0048.

subproblem: caregiver operational work across the care journey
workflow_moment: records appointments communication travel and navigation
claim: The selected accounts describe caregivers performing operational work across record handling, scheduling, navigation, communication, and travel in some oncology journeys.
source_title: De-identified analysis of the expanded pain-point source
supporting_extract: Across the small selected account set, family members participate in several non-clinical coordination tasks; this paraphrase intentionally removes all person and case detail.
method_sample: Three unstructured caregiver accounts in one private source; no standard task inventory, time study, or recruitment method.
limitations: Cannot support the document author's broader claim that caregivers almost always manage operations. No time, frequency, access, consent, digital-fluency, or role-boundary measure is available.
frequency_evidence: Operational caregiver participation appears in selected accounts; prevalence and variation across settings are not measured.
burden_evidence: No caregiver person-time, travel burden attributable to coordination, missed-work measure, or task-completion baseline is reported.
current_workaround: Caregivers use a mixture of personal effort, documents, booking channels, reminders, travel, and communication; exact tools and success are not systematically described.
existing_solution: Care coordinators, navigators, patient portals, appointment systems, and caregiver permissions may support parts of the job; their presence and adequacy are unknown.
contradiction: Caregiver participation is not universal authority. A caregiver-facing workflow could create privacy or access problems if consent and role are assumed.
implication: Treat caregivers as possible workflow actors and research permissioned coordination explicitly; do not replace the named professional owner or infer consent from family relationship.
unknowns: Which tasks recur; who authorises access; which caregivers are involved; person-time; language and digital barriers; current navigator support; measurable operational outcome.
provenance_notes: De-identified paraphrase from a fully reviewed owner-supplied private DOCX. No raw quotation or identifying case combination is retained. Shares one source group with the other V2 account records.

subproblem: digital touchpoints coexist with incomplete workflow
setting: selected oncology care journeys with digital and physical touchpoints
workflow_moment: booking reminders records queues and support access
claim: Selected caregiver accounts contain digital booking, reminder, or retained-record touchpoints alongside queues, coordination friction, or missing family support, showing that feature availability does not establish end-to-end workflow completion.
source_title: De-identified analysis of the expanded pain-point source
supporting_extract: The private account set includes both digital touchpoints and continuing operational or support friction; no exact case narrative is reproduced.
method_sample: Three informal caregiver accounts with no controlled comparison, standard timing method, or system inventory.
limitations: The accounts do not establish causality, frequency, queue duration, product usage quality, or whether different institutions and workflow steps are being compared.
frequency_evidence: Observed only within selected accounts; no service denominator or comparative rate is available.
burden_evidence: No waiting-time, completion, missed-visit, rework, or staff-time baseline is reported.
current_workaround: Digital and manual channels coexist; the exact ownership, integration, and fallback process are not described.
existing_solution: Booking, reminders, and stored records were present in parts of the described journeys but did not by themselves establish counselling access or complete operational flow.
contradiction: Weakens any proposal measured only by feature deployment, messages sent, or records stored. The unresolved problem may be capacity, role clarity, service availability, or another non-software cause.
implication: Evaluate clinic-flow or support candidates using end-to-end completion, waiting, ownership, and burden measures rather than the existence of a digital channel.
unknowns: Exact bottleneck; institution and workflow step; responsible role; baseline waiting/completion; whether integration, staffing, policy, or service capacity is causal.
provenance_notes: De-identified paraphrase from a fully reviewed owner-supplied private DOCX. Exact dates, institutions, people, diagnoses, and clinical narratives remain private. Shares one source group with EV-0045 through EV-0047.

claim: The official CTRI homepage displayed 117,469 registered studies on 2026-09-13; the total covers all registered study types and conditions and is not a count of recruiting oncology trials.
source_title: Clinical Trials Registry–India homepage
publisher: ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health
supporting_extract: The page displayed 'Total Number of Trials Registered in CTRI: 117469' and described the registry as covering interventional, observational, post-marketing, bioavailability/bioequivalence, and postgraduate-thesis studies.
method_sample: Direct observation of the official CTRI homepage on the access date.
limitations: A changing registry counter; broad denominator across diseases and study types; no current cancer-specific or site-recruiting denominator.
frequency_evidence: 117,469 total registered studies displayed on the access date.
burden_evidence: No doctor search time, contact failure, referral burden, or active-site count is reported.
current_workaround: Users search CTRI and may cross-check individual records or other registries.
existing_solution: CTRI is the official free national registry and already provides searchable study records.
contradiction: A large total registry count does not establish the number of relevant or currently recruiting cancer trials and does not justify a new generic repository.
implication: Use the count only with its all-study denominator and access date; derive current oncology inventory separately and label it registry-declared.
unknowns: Current deduplicated recruiting oncology study and site counts; record freshness; contact liveness; user search burden.
provenance_notes: Official page read directly; no record-level or participant data retained.

subproblem: CTRI registration accountability and update workflow
claim: CTRI states that the registrant is the PI or primary sponsor by agreement, the primary sponsor is ultimately accountable, and the lead PI or lead sponsor takes responsibility for multicentre or multi-sponsor registration; registrants receive six-monthly update reminders and can update trial status while other changes may require supporting approvals and field unlocking.
source_title: CTRI FAQ and Important Notice for Trial Registrants
publisher: ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health
supporting_extract: CTRI sends automated reminders every six months, keeps Status of trial permanently unlocked, displays modifications publicly, and specifies email/unlock and EC or DCGI support for certain site, contact, criteria, outcome, and other changes.
method_sample: Direct reading of the official FAQ and registrant notice; the notice was used as the primary locator and the FAQ cross-checked responsibility.
limitations: The pages describe policy and portal process, not actual update timeliness, enforcement effectiveness, site-level verification, or compliance rates.
frequency_evidence: Reminder cadence is six months; no compliance frequency is reported.
burden_evidence: Field unlocking may take 5–7 working days according to the notice; actual delay and staff burden are not measured.
current_workaround: Registrant login, status update, email request, supporting ethics/regulatory material where applicable, and visible modification history.
existing_solution: CTRI already provides an update and audit-trail mechanism.
contradiction: A six-month reminder and registrant-declared status cannot support a real-time site-availability claim.
implication: A product should identify the accountable source party and display declared status separately from time-stamped independent site verification.
unknowns: Update compliance; median time from site change to public record; inactive contacts; enforcement; current unlock performance.
provenance_notes: Official current pages read directly; public contact details were not retained.

subproblem: ClinicalTrials.gov record responsibility and update workflow
setting: ClinicalTrials.gov Protocol Registration and Results System
geography: Global with United States regulatory basis
workflow_moment: record entry approval release review and updating
claim: ClinicalTrials.gov assigns accuracy and release responsibility to the Responsible Party—sponsor, sponsor-investigator, or qualified PI—with a PRS administrator releasing when the sponsor is responsible; recruitment-status changes are due within 30 days for covered records and other submitted information must be reviewed at least every 12 months.
source_title: PRS User's Guide
publisher: ClinicalTrials.gov, U.S. National Library of Medicine
supporting_extract: Authorised users may edit, but the Responsible Party or administrator approves and releases the record for PRS review. PRS review targets apparent errors, deficiencies, inconsistencies, logic, and format; posting is not independent operational verification of a site's ability to enrol.
method_sample: Direct browser reading of the current official PRS User's Guide and cross-check against official quality-control criteria.
limitations: United States legal deadlines apply according to record coverage; the guide does not measure compliance, India-site freshness, or contact liveness.
frequency_evidence: At least annual review; selected changes within 30 days; no observed compliance rate.
burden_evidence: Administrative release and PRS review are described, but actual staff time and site-verification burden are not measured.
current_workaround: Record owners and authorised users edit; Responsible Party or administrator approves/releases; PRS staff review and return issues.
existing_solution: ClinicalTrials.gov already supplies structured international records and documented update governance.
contradiction: Formal update duties and QC do not make the registry a real-time site operations system or establish scientific/site-level truth.
implication: Preserve the Responsible Party and verification date, but obtain separate authoritative site confirmation before representing current availability.
unknowns: India-specific record coverage; update lag; stale-contact rate; cross-registry disagreement; site-confirmation process.
provenance_notes: Official help content read in a real browser because static extraction returned only the page header.

geography: United States guidance transferable to India
workflow_moment: specimen acquisition pathology reporting and selected ancillary testing
claim: NCI describes biopsy or surgery as obtaining tissue for pathologist examination; the pathology report provides definitive cancer diagnosis and commonly histology, grade, margins or lymph-node findings, while selected protein, chromosome, or molecular tests may be included or linked.
source_title: Surgical Pathology Reports
supporting_extract: The pathologist examines tissue or cells from biopsy, surgery, or fluids; fixed tissue is reviewed morphologically, and additional tumour-marker, immunohistochemical, chromosome, or molecular results may be included depending on cancer type.
method_sample: Official patient/professional fact sheet summarising the pathology-report workflow; no cohort or comparative study.
limitations: United States general guidance; actual tests, turnaround, specimen sufficiency, handoffs, and reporting formats vary by cancer, protocol, laboratory, and Indian setting.
frequency_evidence: No workflow frequency is reported.
burden_evidence: Typical fixed-section reporting is described as taking several days and generally within 10 days, but this is not an India baseline and is not used as a target.
current_workaround: Clinicians request biopsy/surgery; pathology processes, examines, and reports; ancillary tests are selectively ordered and linked.
existing_solution: Pathology reports and existing laboratory systems are authoritative source artifacts.
contradiction: The source contradicts a universal serial model of biopsy then PCR then NGS; ancillary tests depend on the case.
implication: Model pathology, focused assays, and broad sequencing as branches with source provenance, not as mandatory sequential product steps.
unknowns: Target-site turnaround, re-biopsy, tissue exhaustion, report-to-oncologist handoff, and trial-specific testing burden.
provenance_notes: Official source read directly; no clinical recommendation or patient detail retained.

subproblem: biomarker assay breadth and non-universal utility
geography: United States guidance transferable to India
claim: NCI states that biomarker tests may examine a single marker, multigene panel, exome, genome, protein, or liquid-biopsy signal; testing can support treatment or trial consideration but is not routine for most patients and may find no actionable match.
source_title: Biomarker Testing for Cancer Treatment
supporting_extract: Some tests check one biomarker and others many; NCI says genomic testing is often suggested for advanced or recurrent cancer and routinely for selected cancers, while biomarker testing may fail because tissue is inadequate, no useful marker is found, or an option is inaccessible.
method_sample: Official explanatory guidance; no universal clinical protocol or India cohort.
limitations: United States treatment and insurance context; testing indications, accepted assays, access, and cost vary by tumour, stage, jurisdiction, and protocol.
frequency_evidence: No population testing rate is reported.
burden_evidence: Cost varies widely; no India price, coverage, turnaround, or staff burden is measured.
current_workaround: Clinician and laboratory select an appropriate validated assay; results are reviewed by the care team.
existing_solution: Single-marker assays, IHC/ISH, multigene panels, liquid biopsy, and linked pathology reports already exist.
contradiction: Biomarker testing can matter for some trials but is not universally necessary and does not by itself establish eligibility or benefit.
implication: For general discovery, a biomarker can be a user-entered search term; interpreting an individual's result or ranking trials remains outside scope.
unknowns: India-specific routine testing pathways; prices; payer coverage; accepted methods; actionable yield; trial-driven re-testing.
provenance_notes: Official source read directly; insurance statements were not transferred to India.

subproblem: tumour NGS indications and accessibility boundary
setting: routine practice and clinical research centres
workflow_moment: decision whether to perform tumour NGS
claim: ESMO's 2024 working-group update recommends tumour NGS for specified advanced cancers, in research centres and specific circumstances, and for tumour-agnostic alterations in metastatic cancers where matched therapies are accessible; it does not recommend broad tumour NGS for every person with cancer.
source_title: Recommendations for the use of next-generation sequencing for patients with advanced cancer in 2024
publisher: European Society for Medical Oncology Precision Medicine Working Group
supporting_extract: The update considered clinical actionability, cost-effectiveness, and accessibility; recommended settings include advanced NSCLC, prostate, colorectal, cholangiocarcinoma, ovarian, advanced breast and selected rare cancers, plus tumour-agnostic alterations where matched therapy is available.
method_sample: Expert working-group recommendations using the ESMO Scale for Clinical Actionability of molecular Targets; published in Annals of Oncology with a 2025 corrigendum.
limitations: Professional guidance, not India-specific; accessibility and cost assumptions vary; recommendations do not determine an individual protocol's accepted assay or eligibility.
frequency_evidence: No India testing frequency is reported.
burden_evidence: Cost-effectiveness and access were considered, but no India price or insurance-denial rate is supplied.
current_workaround: Clinicians and molecular teams select testing under tumour-specific guidance or a research protocol.
existing_solution: Focused tests and tumour NGS already support clinical care and research in selected settings.
contradiction: Directly contradicts the assumption that tumour NGS is a mandatory prerequisite for all oncology trial discovery or all patients.
implication: Keep NGS ordering and interpretation outside the product; record only protocol-stated biomarker requirements in general knowledge views.
unknowns: Indian guideline alignment; local availability; panel price; insurance coverage; turnaround; tissue adequacy; effect on accessible options.
provenance_notes: PubMed abstract read directly; the existence of a 2025 corrigendum is retained.

geography: United States guidance transferable to India
claim: NCI defines tumour-board review as a regularly convened process in which cancer doctors and other specialists discuss new and complex cases to plan treatment; it is not defined as a rare-case-only forum.
source_title: Definition of tumor board review
supporting_extract: The definition names regular review of new and complex cancer cases and a multidisciplinary group that may include medical, radiation and surgical oncologists, pathologists, radiologists, genetics experts, nurses, physical therapists, and social workers.
method_sample: Official terminology definition; no empirical sample or workflow measurement.
limitations: General United States definition; local selection thresholds, attendance, documentation, authority, and follow-through differ. Indian operational prevalence is supplied separately by EV-0019.
frequency_evidence: Regular meetings are described but no rate is measured.
burden_evidence: No preparation time or handoff burden is reported.
current_workaround: Clinicians select and present cases under local policy; specialists discuss and a human team documents the decision.
existing_solution: Local and virtual tumour boards already provide multidisciplinary review.
contradiction: Tumour boards cover more than rare cases, but this does not mean every case is reviewed or that a generic board product is needed.
implication: Ask each target site which cases enter the board and what operational handoff follows; do not generalise a rare-only or all-case rule.
unknowns: Target-site selection criteria; throughput; owner; artefact; acknowledgement; effect of molecular testing on case selection.
provenance_notes: Official definition read through web search because the dynamic dictionary page exposed minimal body text to static extraction.

subproblem: trial discovery screening and formal eligibility boundary
setting: cancer trial search and site screening
geography: United States guidance transferable to India
workflow_moment: gathering cancer details contacting trial team and determining eligibility
claim: NCI's trial-search guidance separates initial search from site assessment: cancer type/stage, prior treatment, tumour genetic changes, age, history, and current health may affect fit; a trial coordinator assesses likely eligibility and a trial-team doctor usually makes the final decision after screening.
source_title: Steps to Find a Clinical Trial and Cancer Details Checklist
supporting_extract: The checklist requests cancer type, primary site, cell type, tumour location/size, stage, prior cancers, performance status, treatments, and marrow/liver/renal tests; the site coordinator discusses likely eligibility, but final determination usually waits for trial-team medical review.
method_sample: Official guidance and a structured checklist, not a validated matching algorithm or minimal-dataset study.
limitations: United States guidance; exact eligibility and accepted evidence are protocol-specific. It does not define a universal minimal dataset or matching accuracy target.
frequency_evidence: No search or eligibility frequency is reported.
burden_evidence: No screening time, false-match rate, or India burden is measured.
current_workaround: Patient/care team gather records, search lists, contact the trial coordinator, and complete site screening.
existing_solution: NCI and ClinicalTrials.gov searches plus trial-site coordinators already support the workflow.
contradiction: A preliminary search result does not equal eligibility; biomarker and treatment history are required only as specified by each protocol.
implication: Keep general discovery separate; any patient-specific comparison requires clinical governance and the trial site retains final eligibility authority.
unknowns: India-specific screening workflow; common missing fields; referral acknowledgement; protocol parsing error; site staffing; current inquiry burden.
provenance_notes: Official page and linked checklist read directly; no individual clinical data used.

subproblem: historical India oncology trial availability and geographic disparity
workflow_moment: geographic trial discovery and availability estimation
claim: A July 2020 CTRI analysis identified 181 open cancer studies, including 132 interventional studies, and reported major interstate disparity; 13 state or union-territory entries had no ongoing study in the authors' analysis.
source_title: Geographic disparities in access to cancer clinical trials in India
supporting_extract: The study estimated state-wise sample size per year from declared target sample, duration, and sites. Reported therapeutic capacity ranged from 0.00 to 296.81 slots per 1,000 incident cancer cases, with no studies in 13 state/UT entries.
method_sample: CTRI records retrieved 15–17 July 2020, manually classified, geocoded by site, and combined with state cancer-incidence estimates; 181 open studies retained.
limitations: Historical registry snapshot; declared open status may not equal live accrual; sample size divided equally across states; incidence data and site addresses required assumptions. The abstract reports median 1.55 while the results text reports 1.02, an internal inconsistency.
frequency_evidence: 181 open studies; 132 interventional; 13 state/UT entries with none in the reported analysis.
burden_evidence: Geographic availability was estimated, but doctor search time, site-contact failure, and referral completion were not measured.
current_workaround: CTRI search, manual cancer classification, address geocoding, and site-by-site interpretation.
existing_solution: CTRI already exposed records; the study built an analytical view of geographic distribution.
contradiction: Shows scarcity and geography can dominate access; an information tool cannot create trial slots. Conflicting median values caution against over-precise reuse.
implication: Use dated counts and preserve the paper's limitations; measure current site verification and do not attribute geographic scarcity to dashboard quality.
unknowns: Current oncology count; true site accrual; capacity allocation; current state coverage; inquiry and referral burden.
provenance_notes: Full article read directly; internal abstract-versus-results median discrepancy explicitly retained.

workflow_moment: registry search analysis and data reuse
claim: A 2019 audit of 12,673 CTRI records reported unclear classifications, internal inconsistencies, incomplete or non-standard information, missing data, name variation, and ethics-committee detail problems; most quantified rates were single-digit but some were higher.
source_title: An analysis of deficiencies in the data of interventional drug trials registered with Clinical Trials Registry - India
supporting_extract: The audit found 1,331 free-text study-type categories, increasing incorrect city listings up to 5.3% in the latest Indian period, name variations, and missing fields; it proposed validation logic, controlled lists, mandatory fields, and standard identifiers.
method_sample: Records downloaded beginning 4 April 2018, reformatted into SQLite, queried with published scripts, and manually cross-checked; analyses focused on selected interventional drug-trial fields and time periods.
limitations: Historical snapshot; selected fields and classifications; some automated interpretations were disputed by CTRI; requirements changed over time; registry quality today may differ.
frequency_evidence: 12,673 registry records were processed; this is not an oncology or currently open denominator.
burden_evidence: Data-cleaning and ambiguity are demonstrated but user time, contact failure, and referral burden are not measured.
current_workaround: Researchers scrape, normalise, manually classify, and cross-check records and ClinicalTrials.gov.
existing_solution: CTRI remains a valuable public registry with modification history and evolving field controls.
contradiction: The findings support data-quality caution but not the blanket claim that CTRI is bad, unusable, or uniformly inaccurate.
implication: A trial view should expose source, field age, ambiguity, and discrepancy rather than silently normalising uncertain data.
unknowns: Current error/completeness rates; oncology subset; contact liveness; status lag; effect of newer controls; user impact.
provenance_notes: Full paper read directly; quantified claims retain their 2018 dataset boundary.

subproblem: CTRI response and limits of automated registry interpretation
workflow_moment: interpreting modifications dynamic sites and missing fields
claim: CTRI-affiliated authors accepted the value of logic and controlled fields but argued that automated analysis can misread audit-trail and dynamic site changes, that legacy records explain some missingness, and that CTRI can request but cannot itself make registrant corrections or enforce updates.
source_title: Letter on: An analysis of deficiencies in the data of interventional drug trials registered with Clinical Trials Registry – India
supporting_extract: The response reclassified several apparent foreign-trial errors using public modifications, described site/ethics fields as dynamic, noted 1,650 registrations before the 2011 revision and about 604 still not updated, and said the registry had no access to edit any data field.
method_sample: Published response from authors affiliated with CTRI, examining examples and operational rules from the audit; not an independent re-audit of all records.
limitations: Registry-affiliated perspective and historical 2020 state; some oversight was acknowledged; it does not establish current quality, update compliance, or live site status.
frequency_evidence: Legacy-record and example counts are supplied; no current compliance rate.
burden_evidence: Manual unlocking and registrant dependence are described, but staff time and update lag are not measured.
current_workaround: CTRI requests correction, validates supporting information, unlocks selected fields, and relies on registrants to update.
existing_solution: Public modification history and later drop-down/logic controls provide context for apparent discrepancies.
contradiction: Directly qualifies EV-0058: not every automated discrepancy is an error, but dependence on registrants still limits freshness and correction authority.
implication: Preserve registry audit history and avoid destructive normalization; represent unresolved discrepancies explicitly and seek site confirmation.
unknowns: Current edit authority; current legacy backlog; enforcement; median correction time; present field validation and completeness.
provenance_notes: Full published letter read directly; author affiliation and lack of independent re-audit retained.

subproblem: Indian investigator recruitment barriers and coordination strategies
workflow_moment: participant recruitment retention and local referral networking
claim: A 73-investigator Indian pilot survey found protocol complexity, patient awareness, and sociocultural issues were frequent recruitment barriers; respondents supported dedicated coordinators, advance recruitment plans, local medical-community interaction, and patient education.
source_title: Challenges in recruitment and retention of clinical trial subjects
supporting_extract: Reported frequent barriers were protocol complexity 38%, lack of patient awareness 37%, and sociocultural issues 37%; 50.7% strongly agreed on a dedicated coordinator and 50.7% agreed on interaction with nearby medical professionals.
method_sample: Pilot online survey February–May 2014; 73 of 128 selected investigators responded. Contacts came from four regions and several specialties; prior communication and private-site overrepresentation limit representativeness.
limitations: Old, small, self-selected, mixed-specialty preference survey; strategies were not tested; no oncology-only, business, referral-completion, or software-effect estimate.
frequency_evidence: Survey proportions describe reported barriers and preferences, not task frequency or population prevalence.
burden_evidence: No person-time, cost, lost revenue, or referral completion baseline.
current_workaround: Investigators use research staff, outreach to nearby clinicians, patient education, and recruitment planning.
existing_solution: Dedicated coordinators and local research networks are established non-product strategies.
contradiction: The dominant barriers may be protocol, awareness, culture, distance, and staffing rather than registry search or matching technology.
implication: Test whether protected coordinator time and a closed-loop referral network solve the job before building automated screening.
unknowns: Current oncology-specific barriers; coordinator funding; off-site referral economics; current contact failure; strategy effectiveness.
provenance_notes: Full article read directly; percentages distinguished from intervention effects.

subproblem: historical India oncology trial institutional incentives
workflow_moment: institutional decision to host oncology trials
claim: A 2013 India oncology review described investigator fees, study grants, infrastructure support, research experience, technology access, training, and patient options as incentives for hosting trials, while identifying clinical overload, staffing, infrastructure, follow-up, and restrictions on academic oncologist remuneration as disincentives.
source_title: Challenges in launching multinational oncology clinical trials in India
supporting_extract: The review names financial incentives such as investigator fees, grants, and infrastructure support, and later says some academic institutions did not allow oncologists to accept remuneration; it also describes research employment, GCP processes, laboratories, and first-hand experience with new drugs as system benefits.
method_sample: Narrative review by Indian and international oncology authors using contemporary literature and experience; not a survey, cost study, or causal evaluation.
limitations: Historical pre-2013 context with many obsolete counts and regulatory/economic assumptions; no off-site referral economics, current site budget, or product willingness-to-pay data.
frequency_evidence: No current frequency or uptake denominator.
burden_evidence: Clinical overload and infrastructure gaps are described, but current cost/revenue amounts are not validly estimated.
current_workaround: Hospitals combine sponsor agreements, investigator effort, research staff, grants, and infrastructure; some academic policies restrict personal remuneration.
existing_solution: Existing sponsor-site contracts and institutional research infrastructure already fund legitimate trial work.
contradiction: On-site incentives do not establish that an off-site referral is financially neutral; neither do they justify informal per-patient referral commissions.
implication: Separate on-site hosting economics from off-site referral economics and validate current institutional policy, reimbursed work, opportunity cost, and return-of-care locally.
unknowns: Current India site budgets; institutional overhead; off-site revenue effect; referral permissions; ethics review; buyer and willingness to pay.
provenance_notes: Full article read directly; all numeric market and cost claims were excluded as obsolete.

subproblem: provider trial screening and off-site referral operations transfer evidence
setting: hospital and academic cancer trial operations
workflow_moment: onsite screening trial offering and offsite referral
claim: A 693-response provider survey reported that onsite screening was mainly manual, the leading stated incentive for offering trials was providing the best options for patients, and off-site referrals were infrequent.
source_title: Provider motivations and barriers to cancer clinical trial screening, referral, and operations: Findings from a survey
supporting_extract: Respondents were primarily physicians and nurses in hospital systems or academic centres; 49.2% screened all patients for onsite trials, 81.9% used manual chart review, 67.7% selected best patient options as the greatest incentive, and the abstract reports offsite referrals were rare.
method_sample: Questionnaire administered to professional societies, advocacy organisations, and industry networks; 693 responses. The survey ran in 2019 and used descriptive statistics.
limitations: Predominantly United States and pre-pandemic; voluntary response; stated practice rather than audit; does not quantify Indian incentives, off-site revenue, search time, or technology effect.
frequency_evidence: Approximately half reported universal onsite screening; offsite referrals described as rare without an abstract denominator.
burden_evidence: Manual screening and administrative barriers are identified, but person-time and financial loss are not quantified.
current_workaround: Manual chart review, provider evaluation, tumour boards, public search tools, and inter-institutional contact.
existing_solution: Institutional research teams and existing search/referral processes already perform this work.
contradiction: Patient benefit can motivate trial offering, but transfer evidence cannot rebut or quantify Indian hospital opportunity cost; the paper's suggested automation remains an unevaluated implication.
implication: Use only as transfer evidence for manual workflow and non-financial motivation; validate India-specific referral behaviour and keep patient-specific automation outside scope.
unknowns: India provider motivation; on-site versus off-site economics; search frequency; current tools; referral acknowledgement; post-2019 changes.
provenance_notes: PubMed abstract read directly; publication date distinguished from the 2019 survey period.

claim: The current CTRI advanced-search interface is a server-rendered HTML form that submits by POST and requires a CSRF token plus CAPTCHA/security code; search by CTRI number also requires human verification, so these pages are interactive access paths rather than a supported machine API.
source_title: CTRI Advanced Search
publisher: ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital Health
supporting_extract: The form posts to advsearch.php, includes hidden csrf_token and __ncforminfo fields, requires a six-character security code sourced from a CAPTCHA endpoint, and returns human-facing record links rather than a documented JSON/XML contract.
method_sample: Direct inspection of the official HTML and form implementation on 2026-09-13; the separate search-by-number page was cross-checked for human verification.
limitations: Absence of a documented API on reviewed pages is not proof that no permissioned or private feed exists. HTML implementation may change without notice; no automated requests were attempted.
frequency_evidence: Not applicable; this is an access-interface observation.
burden_evidence: Interactive search and CAPTCHA create manual effort, but user time and production ingestion cost are not measured.
